On a clear night, the stars seem to twinkle.
But planets usually shine with a steady light. Why?
Starlight crosses space for years without flickering.
The twinkle starts only at the very end, inside our air.
Our atmosphere is full of moving pockets of warm and cool air.
Each pocket bends the light a little differently.
Stars are so far away, they look like single points.
So every tiny bend makes that point jump and blink.
Planets are much closer. They look like tiny disks.
Their many points flicker separately, and the flicker averages out.
